title: Acute coronary syndromes and secondary prevention
blurb: Recognise suspected ACS, give the right immediate treatment, understand STEMI reperfusion windows and support secondary prevention and cardiac rehabilitation.
question: Mr Haddad, 58, has 30 minutes of crushing central chest pain radiating to his jaw, with sweating. His SpO2 is 97% on air and he has no allergies. What immediate treatment should he receive, and what should be avoided?

teach.body: Formally: acute coronary syndromes are unstable angina, NSTEMI and STEMI, caused by sudden reduction in coronary blood flow, usually from plaque rupture and thrombus. In plain English: a coronary artery is suddenly narrowed or blocked. Suspect ACS with chest pain (or pain in the arms, back or jaw) lasting longer than 15 minutes, or chest pain with nausea and vomiting, marked sweating or breathlessness, or with haemodynamic instability.

steps.sub: as soon as possible; do not delay transfer

steps.label: Pain relief
steps.sub: GTN sublingual/buccal; IV opioid if MI suspected

steps.label: Monitor
steps.sub: pain, pulse, BP, rhythm, SpO2, repeat ECGs

teach.caption: If aspirin is given before hospital, send a written record with the person. Other antiplatelets are given in hospital.

values: May be normal or ST depression

values: Angiography within 72 h if risk above low

teach.caption: A normal ECG does not exclude ACS (CG95 1.2.2.5). Serial ECGs help if the diagnosis is in doubt.

children.edge: PCI possible within 120 min of when lysis could be given
children.label: Primary PCI

children.edge: PCI not possible in that time
children.label: Fibrinolysis
children.sub: ECG 60–90 min after; failed? immediate angiography

teach.caption: Assess eligibility immediately, irrespective of age, ethnicity or sex (1.1.1). Level of consciousness after cardiac arrest does not decide eligibility for angiography (1.1.2).

teach.body: Most people with ACS are not hypoxaemic, and unnecessary high-concentration oxygen may increase infarct size. So monitor SpO2 as soon as possible and give oxygen only if SpO2 is below 94% (aim 94–98%); in COPD with a risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, aim for 88–92% until blood gases are available. Also: do not use the response to GTN to make or exclude a diagnosis.

teach.note: Remind people who do not start or stop attending (letter, call or visit). Stable reduced LVEF is not a reason to exclude them from exercise.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Mr Haddad in the emergency department
teach.body: Nurse Leila records a 12-lead ECG within minutes: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF, an inferior STEMI. Mr Haddad receives aspirin 300 mg, GTN and IV morphine for pain. His SpO2 is 97%, so no oxygen is started. The team activates the primary PCI pathway: his pain began 1 hour ago, well within 12 hours. Leila keeps him on cardiac monitoring, reassesses pain and observations, and prepares him for the catheter laboratory.

teach.text: 'MONA' (morphine, oxygen, nitrates, aspirin) for everyone is outdated: oxygen is NOT routine. Also, relief of pain by GTN does not prove the pain is cardiac, and failure to relieve it does not exclude ACS.

items.label: STEMI onset window for primary PCI
PCI vs when lysis could be given

items: Suspect ACS: pain over 15 minutes, or with sweating, nausea, breathlessness or instability.
ECG as soon as possible, aspirin 300 mg, GTN and IV opioid; oxygen only if SpO2 below 94%.
STEMI within 12 hours: primary PCI if deliverable within 120 minutes of when lysis could be given; otherwise lysis.
After MI: ACE inhibitor, DAPT up to 12 months then aspirin indefinitely, beta-blocker, statin.
Cardiac rehabilitation for everyone, starting within 10 days of discharge.

summary: You can now recognise suspected ACS and give the immediate treatment NICE recommends, including why oxygen is not routine. You also understand STEMI reperfusion timing, the secondary prevention medicines after MI and how to support cardiac rehabilitation.

A.q: What dose of aspirin should a person with suspected ACS receive as soon as possible, if not allergic?
A.why: CG95 1.2.3.2 and NG185 1.1.4: a single loading dose of 300 mg aspirin as soon as possible unless allergic.

whyNot.1: 150 mg is not the loading dose.
whyNot.3: 600 mg is not the recommended loading dose.

A.q: A woman with suspected ACS has an SpO2 of 96% on air and no lung disease. What is correct about oxygen?
options: Give 15 L/min via a reservoir mask
Give 2 L/min to protect the heart
Give oxygen if SpO2 is below 94%
A.why: CG95 1.2.3.3: do not routinely give oxygen; monitor SpO2 and offer oxygen if it is below 94% (aim 94–98%) in people not at risk of hypercapnia.

whyNot.0: High-flow oxygen is not routine in ACS.
whyNot.1: Routine low-flow oxygen is still not recommended.
whyNot.2: A Venturi mask is for controlled oxygen in at-risk hypoxaemic patients.

A.q: Which statement about GTN in suspected ACS is correct?
options: Relief by GTN confirms it is angina
No relief by GTN rules out an ACS
A.why: CG95 1.2.1.4: do not use people's response to GTN to make a diagnosis.

whyNot.0: Pain relief by GTN does not confirm a cardiac cause.
whyNot.1: Lack of response does not exclude ACS.
whyNot.3: GTN is given for pain relief as soon as possible, not after troponin.

B.q: A man has a STEMI with symptom onset 3 hours ago. Primary PCI can be delivered within 90 minutes of when fibrinolysis could be given. What is the preferred reperfusion?
B.why: NG185 1.1.6: primary PCI is preferred if presentation is within 12 hours of onset and PCI can be delivered within 120 minutes of when fibrinolysis could have been given.

whyNot.0: Fibrinolysis is for when PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes.
whyNot.2: Medical management is for people ineligible for reperfusion.
whyNot.3: 72-hour angiography relates to NSTEMI, not STEMI.

B.q: After an MI, how long does NG185 recommend dual antiplatelet therapy usually continues?
B.why: NG185 1.4.15: continue dual antiplatelet therapy for up to 12 months after an MI unless contraindicated; aspirin then continues indefinitely.

whyNot.0: 1 month is far shorter than recommended.

B.q: When should a person be invited to their first cardiac rehabilitation session after discharge following an MI?
B.why: NG185 1.8.13: begin cardiac rehabilitation as soon as possible after admission and before discharge, with the first session within 10 days of discharge.

whyNot.2: 3 months is far later than recommended.
whyNot.3: 6 months is far later than recommended.

C.q: Mrs Barnes, 74, has 40 minutes of central chest pain and sweating. Her first ECG is normal. What should the nurse do next?
options: Reassure her that ACS is excluded
Give GTN and discharge if pain eases
C.why: CG95 1.2.2.5–1.2.2.6: do not exclude ACS when the resting ECG is normal; consider serial ECGs and continue monitoring and assessment.

whyNot.0: A normal ECG does not exclude ACS.
whyNot.1: Her symptoms need ongoing hospital assessment.
whyNot.3: GTN response must not be used to make or exclude the diagnosis.

C.q: Mr Patel, 81, had an MI 2 days ago and is now haemodynamically stable. A colleague says he is 'too old' for cardiac rehabilitation. What does NG185 say?
options: Offer rehab once he is fully mobile
C.why: NG185 1.8.1: all people, whatever their age, should be given advice about and offered a cardiac rehabilitation programme with an exercise component.

whyNot.0: There is no upper age limit for cardiac rehabilitation.
whyNot.2: Rehab begins before discharge; mobility is supported within it.
whyNot.3: The programme includes an exercise component, which can be adapted.

C.q: A man treated with fibrinolysis for STEMI has an ECG 75 minutes later showing persistent ST elevation. What does NG185 advise?
options: Wait and repeat ECG in 6 hours
C.why: NG185 1.1.21: ECG 60–90 minutes after fibrinolysis; if residual ST elevation suggests failed reperfusion, offer immediate coronary angiography with follow-on PCI if indicated, and do not repeat fibrinolysis.

whyNot.0: NG185 advises not to repeat fibrinolysis.
whyNot.2: Waiting delays reperfusion of a still-blocked artery.
whyNot.3: GTN does not reperfuse an occluded artery.

reteach.title: Time is muscle
reteach.question: Why does every minute matter in a STEMI, and what does the nurse do in those minutes?

blocks.h: Open the artery, protect the patient
blocks.body: In a STEMI the artery is blocked and heart muscle is dying. The fastest safe way to open it is primary PCI; if that cannot happen within 120 minutes of when clot-busting drugs could be given, fibrinolysis is used. While the team arranges reperfusion, the nurse records the ECG, gives aspirin 300 mg and pain relief, monitors SpO2 (oxygen only if below 94%) and watches for arrhythmias.

blocks.text: Eligibility for reperfusion is assessed regardless of age, ethnicity or sex: older people and women are not offered less.

explain.body: Pain in the chest and/or arms, back or jaw lasting longer than 15 minutes; or chest pain with nausea and vomiting, marked sweating, breathlessness or instability. Assess men and women, and all ethnic groups, the same way.

test.q: Which presentation should make a nurse suspect ACS under CG95?
options: Sharp pain worse on breathing in
Pain reproduced by pressing the chest
A brief twinge lasting a few seconds
test.why: CG95 1.2.1.3: pain in the chest and/or other areas (such as the jaw) lasting longer than 15 minutes, especially with marked sweating, may indicate ACS.

whyNot.0: Pleuritic pain suggests other causes, though ACS is not excluded by a single feature.
whyNot.1: Reproducible chest wall pain suggests a musculoskeletal cause.
whyNot.2: A momentary twinge does not meet the duration criterion.

explain.body: ECG as soon as possible; GTN and IV opioid for pain; aspirin 300 mg; oxygen only if SpO2 below 94%; monitor pain, pulse, BP and rhythm.

test.q: Which analgesia does CG95 recommend, particularly if MI is suspected?
test.why: CG95 1.2.3.1: offer pain relief as soon as possible with GTN, and IV opioids such as morphine, particularly if acute MI is suspected.

whyNot.1: NSAIDs are not the recommended ACS analgesia.
whyNot.2: Paracetamol is inadequate for ischaemic chest pain.
whyNot.3: Entonox is not the CG95 recommendation.

explain.body: STEMI within 12 hours: primary PCI if deliverable within 120 minutes of when fibrinolysis could be given; otherwise fibrinolysis. NSTEMI with intermediate or higher risk: consider angiography within 72 hours.

items.label: NSTEMI angiography if risk above low

test.q: For NSTEMI with an intermediate or higher risk, when does NG185 suggest considering coronary angiography?
test.why: NG185 1.2.13: consider coronary angiography (with PCI if indicated) within 72 hours of first admission for intermediate or higher risk (predicted 6-month mortality above 3.0%).

explain.body: ACE inhibitor (titrated, indefinitely), DAPT up to 12 months then aspirin indefinitely, beta-blocker, statin. Bloods and BP before and 1–2 weeks after starting an ACEi. Rehab for all.

test.q: A man asks how long he should take aspirin after his MI once his second antiplatelet stops. What does NG185 say?
test.why: NG185 1.4.13: offer aspirin to all people after an MI and continue it indefinitely, unless aspirin intolerant or anticoagulation is indicated.

whyNot.0: 12 months is the usual DAPT duration, not aspirin.
whyNot.1: Aspirin is not stopped at 5 years.
whyNot.3: Aspirin does not depend on further angiography.
